
# Methods

## Overview

The accounts deliver five quantities for every reporting year. The **flow without offset** is the CO2 that land removes from the
atmosphere. The **actual flow** is what remains of those removals once the emissions of land are compensated, and it is the service
that reaches society. The **missed flow** is the difference between the two, which is the part of the removals used up by emissions.
The actual flow and the missed flow are also valued in euro. Each quantity is reported in two forms, as tables by country (NUTS0) and
by NUTS2 and NUTS3 region in an Excel workbook, and as maps on a grid of 100 m cells. The section on products at the end describes both.

National greenhouse gas inventories report CO2 by country and land category, and they do not say where on the land it is taken up.
The work therefore runs in four steps, which the sections below follow in order.

1. The inventory gives the removals and the emissions of each land category in each country and year.
2. The offset nets all emissions against all removals across the European Union, and the result is shared among countries. This
   gives the actual flow, the flow without offset and the missed flow by country.
3. A price per tonne of CO2 turns the flows into values, in current prices and in constant prices of 2010.
4. A spatial key, which combines where forest grows with how productive the vegetation is, shares each national value among the
   regions and the 100 m cells of the country. Regions and cells therefore add up to the national values, and they show where
   within a country the service is most likely to occur.

The analysis covers the EU27, by country, NUTS2 region and NUTS3 region under the NUTS 2024
boundaries[, which give {{< fact nuts2 >}} NUTS2 regions and {{< fact nuts3 >}} NUTS3 regions,]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} [@gisco2024nuts]. The boundaries carry the notice © EuroGeographics for the administrative boundaries. All grids use the
projection EPSG:3035, in which every cell covers the same area on the ground[\ (see the stage [`prepare`](#code-prepare) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}.

## Removals and emissions

We took CO2 by source sector from the Eurostat dataset `env_air_gge`[, in the release retrieved on
{{< fact inventory_retrieved >}},]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} [@eurostat2026envairgge] for the 27 Member States and the EU27 aggregate[\ (see the stage [`accounts`](#code-accounts) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}. This dataset
carries the national inventories that countries report under the climate conventions, and its part on land use, land use change and
forestry (LULUCF) gives the CO2 that each land category exchanges with the atmosphere. Following @vallecillo2019, the land categories
are forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other land, which are the codes `CRF4A` to `CRF4F`.

The inventory uses the point of view of the atmosphere, so a negative value is CO2 removed and a positive value is CO2 released. The
accounts reverse the sign, so that a positive balance $b$ of category $k$ in country $c$ is uptake. The removals $R$ and emissions $E$
are the two parts of that balance.

$$
R_{k,c} = \max(b_{k,c},\, 0), \qquad E_{k,c} = \max(-b_{k,c},\, 0)
$$ {#eq-split}

A category that is a net source in a year therefore counts fully as an emission and adds nothing to the removals of that year. Forest
land can be a net source in a country[, as @tbl-sources shows for the reporting years]{.content-visible when-meta="results"}. A category that a country does not report is
set to zero and listed.[\ Among the six land categories, this concerns only other land in Denmark, in
{{< fact dk_other_land_gap_years >}} years.]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} The residual category `CRF4H`[, which {{< fact residual_reporters >}}
of the 27 countries report,]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} stays outside the account.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="results"}
::: {#tbl-sources}
{{< datatable forest_sources >}}

Countries where forest land is a net source of CO2 in the reporting years, in thousand tonnes of CO2.
:::
:::

### Harvested wood products

The inventory reports the change in the stock of harvested wood products as its own category, `CRF4G`. A deduction of that sink from
the removals of forest land is one possible treatment, since the carbon in harvested wood has left the forest. The carbon chapters of
@vallecillo2019 and @lanotte2021 take forest uptake from the inventory as reported and make no such deduction, and the handbook of
Eurostat keeps these products out of net sequestration as a separate category [@eurostat2026handbook, para. 9.56]. A decision was
therefore made not to deduct them. The sink stays outside the flow as a memo item[, at {{< fact balance_CRF4G_2024 >}} million tonnes
in 2024]{.content-visible when-meta="results"}.

## The offset and the actual flow

@lanotte2021 define the service that reaches society as the balance of removals and emissions over all ecosystem types at the level
of the European Union, so an ecosystem type with more emissions than removals provides no service. The EU net flow $N$ is computed
once, over all land categories and countries.

$$
N = \sum_{k,c} R_{k,c} - \sum_{k,c} E_{k,c}
$$ {#eq-net}

@lanotte2021 then attribute this net flow to each country $c$ in proportion to its removals of forest land $R_{F,c}$, in their Equation
6.1. This share is the allocation key of the actual flow.

$$
F_c = N \, \frac{R_{F,c}}{\sum_{c} R_{F,c}}
$$ {#eq-flow}

The flow without offset $W_c$ of a country is the sum of its removals over the six land categories, and the missed flow $M_c$ is the
difference between that and the actual flow.

$$
W_c = \sum_{k} R_{k,c}, \qquad M_c = W_c - F_c
$$ {#eq-missed}

At the level of the European Union, the missed flow equals total emissions by construction. The definition follows from
the distinction that @lanotte2021 draw between the role of forests, shown by removals, and the contribution to society, shown by the
actual flow[\ (see the stage [`accounts`](#code-accounts) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}.

### Choice of the allocation key

The allocation key of @eq-flow is a choice, and a natural alternative exists. Net annual increment is the growth of living trees minus
natural mortality, so it measures forest growth directly and does not depend on the sign that a category takes in the inventory. Every
run compares the two keys[\ (@tbl-comparison)]{.content-visible when-meta="results"}. The compared key shares the EU net flow by the net annual increment of all forest from
Eurostat [@eurostat2026forvolefa], with gaps filled from the nearest years of each country, and it also deducts the sink of harvested
wood products from the removals of forest land. It assigns a flow to countries whose forest land is a net source[, including
{{< fact compared_de_flow_last >}} million tonnes to Germany in 2024,]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} and it can leave countries with a negative missed flow[, between
{{< fact compared_negative_min >}} and {{< fact compared_negative_max >}} in each reporting year,]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} which has no direct reading as a service that is not delivered. The series of net annual increment also carries breaks
between years, and very few countries have reported it for 2024, so most of the key of that year repeats earlier values.

A decision was made to follow Equation 6.1. Under this key no country has a negative missed flow, and a country whose forest land is a
net source receives no flow, which agrees with the definition of the service. [The sink in @tbl-comparison adds up the countries where
the category is a sink, so it is slightly larger than the net balance of the category in the memo item above.]{.content-visible when-meta="results"}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="results"}
::: {#tbl-comparison}

### Allocation to emitting sectors

@vallecillo2019 complement the accounts with a table that attributes the actual flow of each country to the economic sectors in
proportion to their share of its total CO2 emissions, which shows which sectors the service offsets. The attribution does not change the
flow, and it appears in the report of each run only. We grouped the source categories of the inventory into energy supply, manufacturing and
construction, transport, agriculture, forestry and fishing, households, services and other, and waste. These keep the sector names of
the inventory, which differ from the industries of the national accounts, as the fuel that households burn in their cars is reported
under transport.

## Monetary valuation

The value of a flow is the flow in tonnes of CO2 multiplied by a price per tonne. The accounts need a price for the damage avoided by a
tonne of CO2 that stays out of the atmosphere. @vallecillo2019 use the benchmark of EUR 30 per tonne of CO2 from @oecd2016, which they
describe as a reference point and as a lower-end estimate. A decision was made to use a social cost of carbon instead, which is the
value of the damage that one additional tonne causes, because it reflects the long-term damage of climate change and does not depend on
the conditions of a carbon market in a given year.

The value draws on the meta-analysis of published estimates by @tol2023. That work standardises every estimate to 2010 US dollars per tonne
of carbon, for emissions in 2010 [@tol2022], and its update finds a weighted mean of 207 US$ per tonne of carbon, which rises to between 231
and 253 US$ when older studies are discounted [@tol2025]. A decision was made to adopt 266 US$ per tonne of carbon in 2010 prices, which lies
just above that range and well below the kernel mean of 509 US$ in @tol2022, whose long right tail reflects the large uncertainty of these
estimates. We moved it to 2023 prices with the consumer price index of the United States [@bls2023cpi], a factor of 304.70/218.06, and to
euros at the rate of 1.0813 US$ per euro in 2023 [@ecb2023usd]. Those steps lead to about EUR 344, and the accounts use EUR 343.6 per tonne
of carbon. One tonne of CO2 holds 12/44 of a tonne of carbon, so the price per tonne of CO2 is 12/44 of that value in 2023 euros[, or EUR {{< fact price_2023 >}}]{.content-visible when-meta="results"}[\ (see the stage [`prepare`](#code-prepare) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}.

The social cost of carbon is a single real value, so we held it constant in 2023 euros and moved it to the prices of each year $t$ with
the harmonised index of consumer prices $H$ of the European Union [@eurostat2026hicp]. This gives the value in current prices. Constant
prices of 2010 then remove general inflation, so that values of different years can be compared[\ (see the stage [`accounts`](#code-accounts) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}.

$$
P_t = P_{2023}\, \frac{H_t}{H_{2023}}, \qquad V^{\text{current}}_{c,t} = F_{c,t}\, P_t, \qquad
V^{\text{constant}}_{c,t} = V^{\text{current}}_{c,t}\, \frac{H_{2010}}{H_t}
$$ {#eq-value}

[The price moves from EUR {{< fact price_current_2000 >}} per tonne of CO2 in 2000 to EUR
{{< fact price_current_2024 >}} in 2024 in current prices.]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} The missed flow is valued in the same way. The handbook of Eurostat does not
value this service [@eurostat2026handbook].

## The spatial key

The steps so far give national values. Regions and map cells receive a part of them through a spatial key, which gives each place a
weight, and each place takes the national value times its share of the weight of its country.

$$
F_i = F_c\, \frac{w_i}{\sum_{j \in c} w_j}
$$ {#eq-spread}

Because the shares of a country add up to one, regions and cells always add up to the national value, and the key decides only how that
value is distributed within the country.

@vallecillo2019 map forest land only, since it is the one ecosystem type for which almost all countries report uptake, and they spread the
national values with dry matter productivity over the woodland and forest of Corine Land Cover. We followed that approach, with the two more
recent products that the Earth observation roadmap of the same programme names [@zurbaran2025]. The weight of a place is therefore the
forest on it times the productivity of its vegetation.

**Forest** comes from the Corine accounting layers, which the European Environment Agency prepares at 100 m for comparison between years,
in version 21 for all five years [@eea2026clcacc]. The classes are broad-leaved forest (311), coniferous forest (312), mixed forest (313)
and transitional woodland and shrub (324).

**Productivity** is Gross Dry Matter Productivity (GDMP), the rate at which vegetation produces dry matter, estimated from satellite
images by the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service. The annual value is the sum of the 36 ten-day values of the year, each multiplied by its
number of days. The 1 km product, version 2, covers 2000, 2006 and 2012 [@copernicus2020gdmp1km], and it ends in 2020. The 300 m product,
version 2, covers 2018 and 2024 [@copernicus2020gdmp300], and it starts in 2014. Since 2018 exists in both, each run compares them over
the cells of 1 km that are mostly forest.[\ They are {{< fact gdmp_forest_cells_m >}} million cells. The correlation is {{< fact gdmp_pearson >}}, and the mean
of the 300 m product is {{< fact gdmp_ratio_pct >}} percent of the mean of the 1 km product.]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} A difference in level between the products
changes no national total, because the key only shares a national value within a country[\ (see the stage [`prepare`](#code-prepare) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}.

The key takes two forms, which share these ingredients and differ in resolution.

- **The 1 km key** gives the regional tables. Its forest term $S_i$ is the share of the 100 m cells of each 1 km cell that are forest,
  and its productivity $G_i$ is the productivity on the 1 km grid, the mean of the 300 m values within each kilometre in 2018 and 2024
  and the 1 km product interpolated bilinearly to the grid in the earlier years. The weight is $w_i = S_i\, G_i$.
- **The 100 m key** gives the maps. Its forest term is 1 for a 100 m cell of forest and 0 otherwise, and productivity is interpolated
  bilinearly to the 100 m grid.

Both forms place the same national totals. Within a country they agree closely, but they interpolate productivity differently, so the
100 m maps added up over a region can differ slightly from the value of that region in the tables.

## Regional values

NUTS2 and NUTS3 regions receive a share of the national values[\ (see the stage [`prepare`](#code-prepare) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}. The actual flow of a region is the national flow
times the share of the region in the 1 km key of its country. The flow without offset adds up removals of six land categories, and only
one of them is forest, so each category is shared in proportion to the area of that category in the region, according to the Corine
accounting layer of the year. The missed flow of a region is the difference between the two. When a country has no mapped area of a
category, the share of the region in the total mapped land of the country stands in.[\ This concerns only {{< fact fallback_geos >}}.]{.content-visible when-meta="results"}

## Products

**Workbook.** The workbook holds one sheet for each quantity and NUTS level. The sheets of the flow without offset, the actual flow and
the missed flow give thousand tonnes of CO2 and of carbon, and those of the value of the actual and the missed flow give million euro in
current prices and in constant prices of 2010. The reporting years are the columns, and a first sheet explains the contents.

**Maps.** There are five maps for each reporting year on the 100 m grid, built with the 100 m key[\ (see the stage [`maps_100m`](#code-maps_100m) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}. The first is
the actual flow and the second its value at constant 2010 prices. The third is the flow without offset, for which a decision was made to
map the removals of forest land, following @vallecillo2019, because other land categories switch between source and sink across years and
countries and the key places forest only. This map therefore holds less than the flow without offset in the tables, which report the difference by region.[\ In 2024 the
difference is {{< fact no_offset_map_gap_2024 >}} million tonnes.]{.content-visible when-meta="results"} The fourth and fifth are the missed
flow and its value. The missed flow is a balance between removals and emissions and has no place of its own on the land, so a decision
was made to allocate the national value with the key of the actual flow. These two maps show where the removals that compensate emissions
are attributed, and they do not show where any loss of the service occurs.

Each cell holds a whole number in small units, kilograms of CO2 or euro cents at 2010 prices. Whole numbers take about a third of the disk
of decimal numbers, and every country keeps its total to within one part in a thousand. The files are Cloud Optimised GeoTIFF without
overviews, which keeps them small, and a GIS such as QGIS draws them quickly as they are.

**Working layers.** The run also spreads the same national values over the 1 km key. These 1 km layers are not a product of the
accounts. They give the map figures of the report, drawn at 10 km, and the checks of the 1 km key against the tables[\ (see the stage [`maps_1km`](#code-maps_1km) in the code annex)]{.content-visible unless-meta="results"}.

## Checks

The run stops if any check fails. It compares the sectors with total emissions without land use, and the total of land use, `CRF4`,
with the sum of its parts.[\ @tbl-checks records the largest gap of each check. The sectors differ from total emissions without land
use only for {{< fact sector_gap_geo >}} in {{< fact sector_gap_year >}}, where the inventory holds {{< fact sector_gap_mt >}} million
tonnes in the total that it does not hold in the sectors, and this year is not one of the reporting years. The total of land use
equals the sum of its parts in the reporting years, with a largest difference of {{< fact crf4_max_diff >}} thousand tonnes.]{.content-visible when-meta="results"}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="results"}
::: {#tbl-checks}
{{< datatable checks >}}

Consistency checks, with the largest gap and the tolerance that would stop the run. Gaps are relative unless they are marked as absolute.
:::
:::

The 1 km layers are read back from disk and compared with the tables, and the 100 m maps are added up by country from the whole
numbers as they are written and compared with the national values. The run also counts the countries that hold a flow and lack forest
cells, which would lose that flow on the map.[\ The forest area of the 1 km layers is {{< fact forest_grid_mha_2024 >}}
million hectares in 2024, the same as in the table of regions. The largest difference of the 100 m maps from the tables in any year is
{{< fact largest_100m_gap_pct >}} percent. The number of countries that hold a flow and lack forest cells is {{< fact countries_without_forest >}}.]{.content-visible when-meta="results"}
